candidates.title: Kurz's conjecture on the maximum area of the convex hull of a polyhex
candidates.abstract: A polyhex is an edge-to-edge connected system of cells of the regular hexagonal tiling. Kurz (Convex hulls of polyominoes, Beiträge Algebra Geom. 49 (2008), Conjecture 2) conjectured that the convex hull of a polyhex with n cells of unit area has area at most ⌊n² + 14n/3 + 1⌋ / 6. This formalization proves the conjecture, and the sharper bound ⌈n² + 14n/3⌉ / 6, which differs from Kurz's bound by 1/6 when 3 divides n and agrees with it otherwise. The statements are made in the Euclidean plane for the regular hexagonal tiling, with area measured in units of one cell. The proof writes the hull as the hull of the cell centres plus one hexagon, bounds its area through the area of the centre hull and three of its widths, and controls both with a spanning tree of the polyhex. The accompanying paper (arXiv:2609.30310) also shows that the sharp bound is attained for every n by a path made of three straight runs, so that it is the exact maximum. That construction is not formalized.

candidates.title: Lower bounds for the quantum permanent
candidates.abstract: Griffiths's 1969 conjecture on the positivity of Schur forms reduces to the positivity of the quantum permanent $\Phi_n$ on positive bistochastic maps. This conjecture was refuted by Du with a map for which $\Phi_9<0$. Therefore, we ask: how negative can $\Phi_n$ be? We prove a lower bound $\Phi_n\ge-3n/(3n^2+20n+103)$ (for $n\ge 8$), and an asymptotically stronger bound $\Phi_n\ge-1/n+(3e^2-7-o(1))\log n/n^2$. The key to our bounds is the orbital polynomial of the map, which turns $\Phi_n$ into a linear function of a distribution on partitions and positivity into linear constraints. We also construct explicit maps for $n=8, 9$ that improve on Du's example. Finally, if $d_*\in\{4,\ldots,8\}$ is the first dimension for which $\Phi_n<0$, the minimum $\mu_n$ of $\Phi_n$ over positive bistochastic maps satisfies $-\mu_n=\Omega(n^{-d_*})$; we conjecture the matching order $-\mu_n=O(n^{-d_*})$.

candidates.title: A Polynomial Separation for Adaptive Fourier-Overlap Parity Decision Trees
candidates.abstract: Consider the parity decision tree rule that, at every nonconstant restriction, queries a nonzero character maximizing the intersection of the current Fourier support with its translate. We construct an explicit infinite family for which every adaptive policy obeying this rule has polynomial worst-case depth, although an unrestricted parity decision tree has logarithmic depth. For every $\ell\geq1$, let $R=2^\ell$. Our function has $n=4\ell-1+R^2\ell+R$ input bits and exactly $k=R^6-R^5+R$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. Every history-dependent maximizing policy terminates and computes the function, but has a feasible path of length at least $R>k^{1/6}$; an explicit unrestricted tree has depth at most $5\ell\leq\log_2 k$. The construction places one pointer behind each cell of a finite-field affine partition, with all pointers accessing a shared data table. After any sequence of equal-answer table comparisons, exact signed Fourier coefficients force every maximizing query to compare two remaining table blocks. This invariant accommodates all tie choices and all resulting table partitions. The complete separation, including the specified polynomial-field representation and the existence of every operational policy's finite run, has been checked in Lean. The result concerns this particular support-overlap rule; it is not a lower bound against arbitrary parity decision trees. HAL deposit: hal-05800236v1.

Soc. 140 2012, 795 to 804. With G(n) the sum over m1 + m2 = n of Lambda(m1) Lambda(m2), Mathlib's RiemannHypothesis, taken as an explicit hypothesis of the theorem and never as an axiom, implies that the sum over n <= N of G(n) equals N^2/2 - 2 times the sum over nontrivial zeros rho of N^{rho+1} divided by rho times rho+1, plus O(N log^3 N), for N >= 2. The weaker earlier error terms of Fujii, O((N log N)^{4/3}), and of Bhowmik and Schlage-Puchta, O(N log^5 N), follow and are stated too. The zero sum counts zeros with multiplicity, and its absolute convergence is proved unconditionally. Binary Goldbach is open and is not claimed; this is an average over n. An AI agent wrote the Lean code; the statements were checked against the papers by an AI agent and are offered for human audit.

candidates.title: The augmented Descartes theorem in every dimension, its converses, and Soddy's two spheres
candidates.abstract: A Lean 4 development of Section 3 of Lagarias, Mallows and Wilks, Beyond the Descartes circle theorem (Amer. Math. Monthly 109 (2002) 338-361), in the Lorentz form. An oriented sphere in R^n with centre x and signed radius r has the augmented curvature-centre row (|x|^2/r - r, 1/r, x/r); an oriented hyperplane <h, y> = delta with unit normal h has the row (2 delta, 0, h) (LMW Definition 3.2, (3.7)-(3.9)). Tangency is distance-encoded in LMW's oriented sense: two spheres dist^2 = (r + s)^2 (external tangency for two positive radii, internal when one radius is negative), a sphere and a hyperplane <h, x> - delta = -r, two hyperplanes opposite unit normals, LMW's oriented tangency pair by pair, and the converses deliver tangency in this sense; the compatible orientations of an oriented Descartes configuration (disjoint interiors, with the given orientations or all reversed) are proved separately for every solution, after multiplying each row's power polynomial by the total curvature, and for a valid, pairwise tangent family with positive total curvature for its own open interiors. Kernel-checked, for every n >= 1 (LMW's Section 3 assumes n >= 2; their Section 8, (8.4), is the identity on the line): the augmented matrix W of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres of nonzero curvature, and of n + 2 pairwise tangent spheres and hyperplanes, satisfies W^T Q_n W = [[0, -4, 0], [-4, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2 I_n]] with Q_n = I - (1/n) 11^T (Theorem 3.3); every real solution W is the augmented matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes, and, when its second column has no zero, of exactly one pairwise tangent family of spheres (the converse of Theorem 3.3); the Soddy-Gosset relation (sum 1/r_i)^2 = n sum (1/r_i)^2 with and without hyperplanes (Theorem 1.2, (1.2)) and its form b^T Q_n b = 0 ((3.2)); the curvature-centre identity M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) (Theorem 3.2, (3.5)); at n = 2 the complex Descartes theorem (sum b_i z_i)^2 = 2 sum (b_i z_i)^2 and sum b_i (b_i z_i) = (1/2)(sum b_i)(sum b_i z_i) (Theorem 2.1, (2.2)-(2.3)); det Q_n = -2/n; and the three statements for Mathlib's EuclideanGeometry.Sphere (pairwise IsExtTangent, or one enclosing sphere to which the others are IsIntTangent, with curvature -1/r_e). The matrix identity is proved as LMW's Section 4 argument (Lemmas 4.3-4.4, (4.9)-(4.10)) run directly in Euclidean coordinates: W^T Q_n W is the target exactly when the rows of W have Lorentz norm 1 and pair to -1 under G = [[0, -1/2, 0], [-1/2, 0, 0], [0, 0, I_n]], since W G W^T = 2I - J and (2I - J)(Q_n/2) = I. Also proved: both halves of the converse of the Soddy-Gosset theorem, LMW's Theorem 3.1, about which they write "We do not know an easy proof of this result; a proof appears in [16]" ([16] is Graham-Lagarias-Mallows-Wilks-Yan III, whose arXiv versions 1-2 prove both halves as their Theorem 2.2 from the same base configuration and the transitivity of the Lorentz group, a section the published version omits). Existence: every nonzero b with (sum b_i)^2 = n sum b_i^2 is the curvature vector of a pairwise tangent family of spheres, where b_i is nonzero, and hyperplanes, where b_i = 0, and of a family of spheres when no b_i vanishes, by one Q_n-reflection from the configuration of two parallel hyperplanes and n unit spheres in the proof of GLMWY III's Theorem 6.1, or from its inversion in the unit sphere. Congruence: two valid, pairwise tangent families with the same curvatures, index by index, are carried one to the other by exactly one Euclidean motion x -> x O + t with O^T O = I, reflections and hyperplanes included, with O = (1/2) X^T Q_n X' and t = -(1/4) a^T Q_n X' for augmented matrices [a | b | X] and [a' | b | X'] and the motion's action on points, spheres and hyperplanes; W_1^-1 W_2 preserves the target form and fixes the curvature coordinate, and every such matrix is a motion matrix (GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 argue instead by the rigidity of a simplex of centres); its uniqueness and parameters are proved here. A motion preserves validity, curvature and tangency, so two valid, pairwise tangent families are congruent exactly when their curvature vectors agree. For every solution W: the total curvature B is nonzero, the open sets {y : B F_i(y) < 0}, F_i(y) = b_i |y|^2 - 2 <v_i, y> + a_i the power polynomial of row i (negative exactly inside a ball, outside a ball of negative radius, or on the side of a hyperplane its normal points to), are pairwise disjoint, at most two rows are hyperplanes, and no three boundaries pass through a finite point; for a valid, pairwise tangent family the total curvature is nonzero, at most two members are hyperplanes, and when the total curvature is positive the open interiors are pairwise disjoint. The converse of Theorem 3.2 in every dimension under the hypothesis of a nonzero first column (every real M with M^T Q_n M = diag(0, 2 I_n) and a nonzero first column is the curvature-centre matrix of exactly one family of valid, pairwise tangent oriented spheres and hyperplanes), which GLMWY I, Theorem 3.1 and its Remark, prove at n = 2 with that hypothesis and which LMW's printed converse ("any real solution M") and GLMWY III's arXiv v1-v2 Theorem 2.3 omit, together with the matrix at n = 2 with columns 0, e_0 - e_1, e_2 - e_3 (GLMWY I's configuration (3.15) with its first column zeroed; the matrix of four oriented lines with normals +-e_0, +-e_1), which solves the equation and is the curvature-centre matrix of no valid, pairwise tangent family. The existence of a configuration in every dimension (that configuration); for n >= 2 the Apollonian generators S_k = I + (2/(n-1)) e_k 1^T - (2n/(n-1)) e_k e_k^T of GLMWY III, (4.1), preserve Q_n and carry configurations to configurations, with the row formula (S_k W)_k = (2/(n-1)) sum_{i != k} W_i - W_k, and Soddy's two spheres (LMW, footnote 3; GLMWY III, Section 4.1), in the signed sense: the oriented spheres and hyperplanes tangent to n + 1 members of a configuration are exactly the missing member and its Apollonian reflection, two distinct objects whose curvatures sum to (2/(n-1)) times the sum of the others' curvatures. The planar Soddy-Gosset relation for four circles of positive radius, pairwise externally tangent or with one enclosing circle, is already in Lean in facebookresearch/atlas-lean (descartes_circle_theorem, not registered); rjwalters/lean-genius and carlok/LeanFrontier treat the planar relation as a definition (its two roots, the same over the complex numbers, integer reflections and parity; LeanFrontier checks it for one family of Ford circles and their tangent line), with no derivation from tangency; no other formalization of these statements was found by the dated searches.

candidates.title: Erdos607
candidates.abstract: Machine-checked upper bound on Erdős problem 607. For n ≥ 2 let F(n) be the number of distinct multiplicity sets A(P) that can arise from a collection P of n points of the plane, where A(P) is the set of block sizes (point counts) of the lines determined by P. The proof shows that the lines of P form a pairwise-balanced design on the n points (every pair of points lies on exactly one line, and each line contains at least two points), so A(P) is exactly the set of block sizes of such a PBD. Hence F(n) is bounded by the number of PBD profile sets on n points, and the Colbourn–Phelps–Rödl (1984) Theorem 2.4 bound exp(c·√n) on that quantity gives F(n) ≤ exp(c·√n) for every n ≥ 2. The bound is stated for n ≥ 2 — the range where the bound is meaningful (a single point determines no line) — so the hypothesis is non-vacuous. The CPR-1984 PBD bound is a published theorem and is taken as the hypothesis hCPR; it is cited, not re-proved here. Together with the Szemerédi–Trotter (1983) lattice-grid lower bound F(n) ≥ exp(c'·√n) (also cited, not re-proved), the order of growth is F(n) = exp(Θ(√n)). This repository contains zero axioms and zero sorry in the proof development (the only sorry is the deliberate statement surface in Challenge.lean).

candidates.title: Chemical heredity without genetic templates
candidates.abstract: Acquisition and retention of catalytic function are established for a four-compartment chemical model with three prescribed catalyst types and finite resources. Starting with at least 512 copies of each of two old catalyst types per compartment, arbitrary candidate counts and arbitrary fuel occupancy, a seeding phase ends at time 30. At the fixed beta = 4,000,000 operating point, the joint mission through time 60 has failure probability at most 0.004517975690072193. It includes applicable count floors of 16 for both actual complementary daughters, 3,000,000 service credits, at least five initiating divisions per compartment after seed withdrawal, and eleven current-population recoveries interleaved with ten selected actual divisions by time 55.5. Seven simultaneous resource ceilings are enforced by one finite-stock process, with the first attempted excess entering failure. The proof connects the marked physical-time law, deterministic seed withdrawal, stopped recovery and resource accounting to the complete mission.

candidates.title: Nonlinear Wave Limits of Reversible Finite-State Cellular Automata
candidates.abstract: We construct reversible finite-state cellular automata whose integer lifts approximate smooth solutions of one-dimensional semilinear wave equations. The kick–drift update is bijective for every odd modulus. Separate rounding of spatial edge contributions and local nonlinear forces gives an exact one-cell support bound for the full local operator algebra. Under a strict Courant condition, a discrete energy estimate bounds the field and staggered-velocity errors by $C_T(h^2+\tau^2+\delta/\tau^2)$ on a fixed physical time interval, where $h$, $\tau$, and $\delta$ are the spatial, temporal, and field spacings. An explicit modulus bound prevents modular wrapping throughout that interval. The choices $\tau=\nu h$, $0<\nu<1$, and $\delta=O(h^4)$ yield second-order convergence. Coupled scalar fields have a common-speed, locally Lorentz-covariant classical limit. Equal bare masses and equal quartic self-couplings preserve a symmetric invariant manifold. Unequal quartic couplings introduce a cubic source into the antisymmetric field equation, and we derive the first variation of the antisymmetric field. Numerical experiments compare exact integer trajectories with a nonlinear traveling wave and an independent continuum solver, measure light and massive dispersion branches, and examine continuously interacting wave packets. The accompanying programs reproduce the reported calculations.

candidates.title: The additive theorem for 2-transitive Galois groups (Girstmair; Dixon, Theorem 1') and its representation-theoretic engine
candidates.abstract: Kernel-checked proofs, in Lean 4 + Mathlib, of the homogeneous case and, at the roots, of the printed form (relations with value in K), with coefficients in any field K of characteristic 0, of the additive theorem for 2-transitive Galois groups (Girstmair, Manuscripta Math. 39 (1982) 81-97, Proposition 4, Assertion 3, p. 86, for every field whose characteristic does not divide |G|; stated by J. D. Dixon, Acta Arith. 82 (1997) 293-302, as Theorem 1', p. 301, with its proof omitted), of its representation-theoretic engine (classical: Huppert, Endliche Gruppen I, p. 597, Satz 20.2, as cited by Girstmair, Acta Arith. 89 (1999) 53-96, p. 78; used by Dixon on p. 297, in the proof of Theorem 1(ii), citing Curtis-Reiner Section 32B), and of two criterion forms over any field whose hypothesis is the irreducibility of the augmentation module instead of 2-transitivity (the 'if' direction of Girstmair 1982, Proposition 4, Assertion 2, in its module form). Eight compared theorems, in namespace DixonRelations, in this order. (1) zeroSum_irreducible, the engine: for a finite group G acting 2-transitively on a finite set Omega with 2 <= |Omega| and a field K of characteristic 0, the augmentation (zero-sum) subspace V0 = {f : Omega -> K | sum_x f x = 0} of the permutation module Omega -> K is an irreducible K[G]-module; proved in the substantive form of simplicity, that a G-invariant subspace W <= V0 with W != bot equals V0. The G-action is the permutation representation (g . f) x = f (g^{-1} . x), and a subrepresentation is a Submodule together with an explicit invariance hypothesis. (2') additive_core_of_irreducible, the zero-sum criterion form: for any field K, any group G (finite or not) acting on a finite Omega, an injective family alpha : Omega -> L into a K-vector space L, K-linear maps phi g with phi g (alpha x) = alpha (g . x) (no homomorphism property assumed), and the hypothesis hirr (every nonzero G-invariant K-subspace of V0 is V0, word for word the conclusion of (1); it holds vacuously when V0 = 0, that is |Omega| <= 1), any c with sum_x c x = 0 and sum_x c x . alpha x = 0 is 0. (2) additive_core, the zero-sum form for an abstract family: the same conclusion for K of characteristic 0 and a finite group G acting 2-transitively on Omega with 2 <= |Omega|; it is (1) followed by (2'). (3) additive_roots_no_relation, the zero-sum form at the roots: for K of characteristic 0 and an irreducible f in K[X] of degree >= 2 whose Galois group acts 2-transitively on the roots of f in the splitting field, any K-valued coefficient tuple c on the roots with sum_r c r = 0 and sum_r c r . r = 0 is 0; G = f.Gal, Omega = f.rootSet f.SplittingField (with Mathlib's instance Polynomial.Gal.galActionAux), the family is the inclusion of the root set, phi g is the field automorphism g read as a K-linear map (the compatibility holds by rfl), and 2 <= |Omega| follows from card_rootSet_eq_natDegree with separability from Irreducible.separable; f.SplittingField appears in the 2-transitivity hypothesis and in the types of c and of the relation hypothesis. (3) is the zero-sum part (value 0, coefficient sum 0) of the homogeneous case of Dixon's Theorem 1' at the roots; the full homogeneous case at the roots is (5), and the inhomogeneous case is (6). (4') relModule_le_span_one_of_irreducible, the span-one criterion form: under the hypotheses of (2') and a transitive action, every coefficient tuple c with sum_x c x . alpha x = 0 is a scalar multiple of the all-ones tuple, i.e. relModule K alpha is contained in the line K . (fun _ => 1). This is the 'if' direction of Girstmair 1982, Proposition 4, Assertion 2 (p. 86: "If G is primitive on G/H, (G,H) admits only trivial relations over K iff the complementary module U(G/H) of K epsilon_0 is simple"), whose hypothesis is, like hirr, the simplicity of a module; Girstmair 1999 restates it in character form as Proposition 12 (p. 78), "essentially contained in Proposition 4 of [11]". (4') assumes transitivity in place of primitivity; for a transitive action, hirr already forces primitivity (elementary, not formalized: the zero-sum functions constant on the blocks of a nontrivial block system form a nonzero proper invariant subspace of V0), so the difference is one of form only. (4) relModule_le_span_one, the span-one form: the same conclusion under the hypotheses of (2); it is (1) followed by (4'). (5) relModule_roots_le_span_one, the span-one form at the roots: under the hypotheses of (3), relModule K of the root family (fun r => (r : f.SplittingField)) is contained in K . (fun _ => 1); it is (4) at the roots. (6) roots_inhomogeneous_iff_const, Dixon's printed form at the roots: under the hypotheses of (3), sum_r c r . r = algebraMap K f.SplittingField k for some k in K if and only if c is constant; in Dixon's notation this is U = K.e. Dixon's Theorem 1' is stated for any subfield K of C and for relations with value in K; compared statements (2), (3), (4) and (5) concern its homogeneous case (value 0) and (6) its printed form (value in K), for every field K of characteristic 0, and (2') and (4') take any field. Girstmair 1982 states the additive theorem for every field whose characteristic does not divide |G|, so characteristic 0 is a sub-case of his hypothesis; (2') and (4') take any field, but their content is carried by hirr, which this entry proves only in characteristic 0 and only for 2-transitive actions, as (1). An uncompared bridge, BDS.isAtom_zeroSumSubrep_iff, shows that hirr together with V0 != bot is atomicity of V0 in Mathlib's lattice of subrepresentations of the permutation representation on Omega -> K. (1) is proved by an elementary, character-free stabilizer-averaging argument; Dixon (p. 297) cites Curtis-Reiner Section 32B for the statement only; Curtis-Reiner was not consulted, and nothing is claimed about its proof. (2') applies hirr to relModule K alpha meet V0 and uses injectivity of alpha; (4') shows that a relation and each of its translates differ by a zero-sum relation, so the relation is G-invariant, hence constant by transitivity (no averaging); the forward direction of (6) argues in the same way at the roots for a relation with value in K, using (2), and its reverse direction uses that the sum of the roots of a separable polynomial is fixed by every automorphism of the splitting field, which is Galois over K, and so lies in K. This formalizes classical results; it is not new mathematics. Research context: additive and multiplicative relations among conjugate algebraic numbers are studied in Girstmair (1982, 1999), Smyth (1986), Drmota-Skalba (1991), Baron-Drmota-Skalba (1995), Dixon (1997) and Zheng (2021); in the sources read for this entry the doubly transitive additive case is derived from the criterion and character theory in one sentence (Girstmair 1982, p. 86), set aside because the doubly transitive pairs are classified (Girstmair 1999, p. 78), and stated with its proof omitted (Dixon 1997, p. 301); this entry gives a complete, character-free, machine-checked proof. The namespace BDS of the two entry definitions is the development's historical name (after Baron-Drmota-Skalba); no result of Baron-Drmota-Skalba is formalized. Formalization status (search of 2026-10-28 for the six statements (1), (2'), (2), (3), (4') and (4) as stated here, at the repository heads listed in README.md; a search result, not a guarantee): none of the six statements searched was found in any prover; (5) and (6), searched for on 2026-10-29 at the repository heads listed in README.md, were not found either. The fact behind the reverse direction of (6), that the sum of the roots lies in the base field, is in Mathlib at the pin in Vieta form (Polynomial.Splits.nextCoeff_eq_neg_sum_roots_mul_leadingCoeff), for the multiset of roots. The S_n case of (1) is formalized in augmentation form over every field in which |Omega| != 0 (every field when |Omega| = 2), in particular over Q, in TauCeti (TauCeti.isIrreducible_standardRepresentation, since 2026-08-05) and as Specht-module irreducibility over C in openai/math; the general 2-transitive case of (1) is formalized in character form over C in AxiomMath/CFSG (CFSG.permutation_character_orbit_count, public since 2026-10-27), the closest item found: CFSG also defines the same V0 over C under the same action (CFSG.Wreathed.CentralSL2.sumZeroSubrep) and computes its character, from which the C case of (1) in submodule form would follow in a few lines, but no theorem stating it was found. NOT formalized and NOT claimed: the MULTIPLICATIVE theorem (Dixon Theorem 1(ii), and, per Zheng 2021, arXiv:1912.07202v1, p. 2, Baron-Drmota-Skalba 1995, Theorem 3), under which 2-transitivity does NOT force triviality: for a prime p and b in Q not a p-th power, X^p - b has Galois group AGL(1,p) over Q, acting sharply 2-transitively on the roots, and the ratios of its roots are p-th roots of unity, nontrivial multiplicative relations; Dixon's Theorem 1(ii) gives necessary conditions for that exception; none of that multiplicative content is proved or claimed here. The additive theorem carries no such exception, because the additive module cannot contain any e_gamma - e_delta (Dixon, p. 301). Also not formalized: the 2-transitivity of any particular Galois group (a hypothesis in (1), (2), (3), (4), (5) and (6)); any case of hirr other than the 2-transitive one, (1); the imprimitive case (Girstmair 1982, Proposition 4, Assertion 1; Girstmair 1999, Proposition 12, first sentence) and the fact that hirr forces primitivity for a transitive action; the 'only if' direction of the criterion, the character form of its hypothesis, and the converse of Assertion 3 that Girstmair 1982 states for a splitting field; and the identification of Omega -> K with the scalar extension of Omega -> Q.

candidates.title: Hermite's signature theorem and the coprime compositum, with the degree-12 compositum of x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1
candidates.abstract:
Kernel-checked proofs, in Lean 4 + Mathlib, of six general theorems and twelve statements about one number field. General: (1) Hermite's signature theorem for every real polynomial f, degenerate case included and with no monic hypothesis: the power-sum Hankel (Hermite) form H_f has sigPos = #R + #C+, sigNeg = #C+, rank sigPos + sigNeg = #D and radical of dimension deg f - #D, where D, R, C+ are the distinct complex roots, the real ones, and those in the upper half plane; (2) its number-field form (classical, Hermite-Sylvester; in number-field form credited to O. Taussky 1968): the trace form Tr_{K/Q}(x^2) of a number field K has type (r1 + r2, r2), and is positive definite iff K is totally real; (3) the places of a linearly disjoint compositum L = K1 K2: r1(L) = r1(K1) r1(K2) and 2 r2(L) = [K1:Q][K2:Q] - r1(K1) r1(K2); (4) the signed discriminant of such a compositum with coprime discriminants, d_L = d_{K1}^[K2:Q] d_{K2}^[K1:Q], the sign included; (5) the trace projection [E:F]^-1 Tr_{E/F} onto a subfield F, the orthogonal decomposition E = F + F^perp for Tr_{E/Q}(xy) with F^perp = ker Tr_{E/F}, the restriction of the trace form of E to F as [E:F] times the trace form of F, and the type (r1(E) + r2(E) - r1(F) - r2(F), r2(E) - r2(F)) of its restriction to ker Tr_{E/F}; (6) the squarefree-discriminant criterion (a textbook exercise). Loeffler) and, for (2) and (5), Algebra.traceForm, between which Mathlib has no theorem at the pinned revision; (3) and (4) from Mathlib's infinite places and linear disjointness. The proof modules also prove, not compared, that sigPos and sigNeg are additive over orthogonal direct sums and invariant under positive scaling over any linearly ordered field, and that the signature of a rational matrix form is unchanged by base change to R; Mathlib at the pin has none of these. Mathlib prior art is used and not re-proved: X. Roblot's theorem on the absolute value of the discriminant of a coprime compositum (statement (4) adds the sign) and his theorem on its ring of integers (used in (8)). The definiteness corollary of (1) (real-rooted iff H_f positive semidefinite) was formalized in Lean 4 by P. Alexandersson (RealRooted, 2026-09-27) before this entry; (1) proves the full rank/signature/radical count, from which that corollary follows. Application (cited, not a claim of the entry): In the author's Pisot Dimensional Theory, Q(rho) is the arithmetic of three-dimensional space and Q(Q) the arithmetic of four-dimensional spacetime, and their compositum K is the parent of both. Read through the theory, this entry's theorems make six conclusions exact.
Space and spacetime are the only worlds the parent contains. The fields between Q and K have degrees 3 and 4 and no others: Q(rho) and Q(Q) are K's only proper subfields other than Q (16). An intermediate sub-arithmetic of the parent has dimension 3 or 4, and nothing else; there is no 2-, 6- or other intermediate world.
The world is a product, not a sum. K is the tensor product of the two sectors, 12 = 3*4 (7), and its integers are exactly Z[rho] (x) Z[Q] (8). The parent's discrete structure is built from the two sectors' lattices and nothing else.
The parent's geometry is the product of space's and spacetime's. The trace form of K has type (7,5) (10), and it is the tensor product of the sectors' own forms (PALOMAR-2026-09-02-000014): (2,1) (x) (3,1), with 2*3 + 1*1 = 7 and 2*1 + 1*3 = 5. On the quartic sector the form is 3 times spacetime's own, of Lorentzian type (3,1); on the cubic sector, 4 times space's, of type (2,1) (13). The one time direction is not put in by hand: it is what the parent's form is on spacetime.
All of the parent's asymmetry between space and time is spacetime's. The parent's excess of positive over negative directions, 7 - 5 = 2, is exactly spacetime's 3 - 1 = 2. The eight dimensions orthogonal to spacetime are perfectly balanced, four positive and four negative (5, 13).
Both sectors are recovered from the parent. The relative traces, divided by the relative degrees [K:Q(rho)] = 4 and [K:Q(Q)] = 3, are the orthogonal projections onto the sectors (5), and the traces themselves carry the parent's lattice onto Z[rho] and Z[Q] (12). Every element of space and of spacetime is the shadow of an element of the parent.
The parent is built from minimizers, and joining them creates nothing smaller. Each sector's generator is a minimizer, certified in the author's registered entries: x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1 attain the least Mahler measure above 1 among irreducible integer polynomials of degrees 3 and 4 (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004); rho is the least Pisot eigenvalue of any substitution on at most three letters, the slowest settling clock (PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000019), and the growth rate of the triangle group (2,3,infinity) = PGL(2,Z), the slowest of the hyperbolic triangle groups (p,q,infinity) (PALOMAR-2026-10-17-000013). K is the compositum of the two minimizers, and a single number generates all of it: rho*Q, the theory's coupling ruler (15; PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005). Minimality survives the join. No element of K other than +/-1 has a conjugate on the unit circle (17), so the parent contains no Salem number, and with Smyth's theorem every nonzero integer of K other than +/-1 has Mahler measure at least rho (18), with equality at rho itself (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004). The 3D generator is the smallest nontrivial size in the whole twelve-dimensional arithmetic, exactly as in degree 3. In the theory, rho is the ground of minimality and therefore the ground of three-dimensional structure; joining space to spacetime keeps that ground.
The two sectors are the two sides of the Pisot boundary. rho is a Pisot number, and the Padovan substitution tiling, whose characteristic polynomial is x^3 - x - 1, is a regular model set with pure-point diffraction (Baake and Grimm 2020): the ordered, classical sector. It is handed, the arrow of time: its tiling flow is neither mutually locally derivable from nor topologically conjugate to its mirror image (Gaehler 2026, Example 10 and Remark 7, where the Padovan rule is varrho_R after renaming a <-> c), and in the factor language the author's registered entries PALOMAR-2026-08-19-000006, PALOMAR-2026-09-04-000004 and PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000019 certify it: ca occurs and ac never does. Q is not Pisot (PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000012), and every primitive self-similar tiling of the line with expansion Q has no non-trivial pure-point spectrum (Solomyak 1997): the quantum sector, which cannot settle on a line. This is the arithmetic of a quasicrystal (superspace crystallography: de Wolff 1974; Janner and Janssen 1977; cut-and-project: de Bruijn 1981; Kramer and Neri 1984; Duneau and Katz 1985; Elser 1986): a higher-dimensional lattice, O_K in R^2 x C^5, from which the sector lattices are recovered by the traces (12).

candidates.title: Hamilton cycles in Cayley graphs of polylogarithmic degree
candidates.abstract: A complete Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the following theorem: there are absolute constants C, n0 > 0 such that every connected Cayley graph Cay(G, S) on n >= n0 vertices whose degree d = |S| is at least C (log n)^13 / log log n contains a Hamilton cycle (Lovasz.hamiltonian_of_polylog_degree). Here G is a finite group, S is a connection set (S = S^-1 and 1 not in S, so the graph is |S|-regular), log is the natural logarithm, and connectivity is equivalent to S generating G. The theorem is a case of the Lovász conjecture (every connected vertex-transitive graph has a Hamilton path) in its Cayley-graph form (every connected Cayley graph on at least three vertices is Hamiltonian). For arbitrary connected Cayley graphs the previously published degree thresholds were linear degree (Christofides, Hladký and Máthé, 2014) and degree at least n^(1-c) (Bedert, Draganić, Müyesser and Pavez-Signé, 2026). The proof follows the source manuscript: it extracts a connected bipartite template with spectral gap of order (log n)^-2, allocates the vertices to weighted translates of the template by signed rounding (a robust signed integrality theorem derived from the capacitated b-matching polytope, swap rounding, and a trace-exponential matrix concentration bound), connects the pieces by a sparse matching chosen by mutual nominations and a signed circulation, absorbs the outside matching inside every piece with Hamilton routers built from even-cycle comparators, and merges cycles. Every lemma of the manuscript is proved in the repository, as are the classical results it uses without proof (normalized Cheeger inequality, Haxell's hypergraph matching theorem, the b-matching polytope, Watkins's connectivity bound, the Nash-Williams–Tutte tree-packing theorem, Hoffman's circulation criterion, scalar Chernoff bounds); Hall's theorem is taken from Mathlib, and matrix Bernstein is avoided by deriving the one lemma that used it from the manuscript's own concentration bound. The source manuscript is an unpublished research draft that describes its own proof as not independently verified; this formalization is, to the maintainer's knowledge, the first verification of the theorem. The proved theorem has no sorry and depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

candidates.title: Selection of the electromagnetic source tensor by covariance, conservation and the exchange law
candidates.abstract: On a fixed flat Lorentz frame with metric diag(1,1,1,-1), sources are symmetric 4x4 tensor-valued functions of the six real components of an antisymmetric field. Twelve kernel-checked statements. Among all symmetric homogeneous quadratic sources (210 free coefficients), the six infinitesimal Lorentz covariance equations together with zero trace select the Maxwell stress (the electromagnetic energy-momentum tensor) up to a unique real scale, and a displayed certificate of 209 linear coefficient equations is equivalent to both laws. Among the same homogeneous quadratic sources, conservation alone - vanishing divergence on every source-free Maxwell/Bianchi first jet - selects the same line, with covariance, trace zero and Hodge invariance derived rather than assumed. The globally C^3 symmetric conserved sources are exactly an explicit seventeen-parameter family (constant, a six-parameter cross term, and the stress), and with covariance zero field value is equivalent to zero trace and to the stress line. Under the sourceful exchange law at current stiffness k (the real factor multiplying the jet current), every everywhere-differentiable symmetric source is a constant plus the Maxwell stress of scale exactly k, and conversely, with no polynomial, degree, C^3, covariance or trace hypothesis; zero field value selects the stress. Explicit counterexamples show that covariance and zero trace are each necessary in the quadratic selection, and that covariance and the zero-field normalization are each necessary in the C^3 selection. Uniqueness of the Maxwell stress tensor is classical (Fock 1964; Kerrighan 1982; Navarro-Sancho 2012; the classification of Maxwell conservation laws by Anco-Pohjanpelto 2001); the contribution is the constructive, kernel-checked development on the explicit register at finite regularity, with finite certificates, the covariance-free routes, and the differentiable-only sourceful statement. Pisot Dimensional Theory motivates the frame; no physical coupling is selected.

candidates.title: shaikidris/prime-star-spectra-formalization
candidates.abstract: A Lean 4 formalization of the ordered adjacency spectrum of finite prime-cover graphs. Its root-centred specialization proves that the square of the largest ordered eigenvalue equals pi(X) plus four times the finite prime sum of 1/(p-1), up to o(1). More generally, for every fixed finite set S of deleted primes and epsilon > 0, the same law with the explicit centre correction c(a) holds uniformly over allowed centres a <= (log X)^(1/2-epsilon). The same window admits a uniform centre--shell evolution theorem at the explicit first-exit frequency, with a finite localization-plus-phase error bound.

candidates.title: Infinite rank of the three-prime running-LCM kernel
candidates.abstract: For pairwise distinct primes p, q and r, the three-prime reciprocal running-LCM kernel has nonzero square minors of every order, with row and column indices chosen independently of the third exponent. Consequently it admits no finite rational separated representation. The selected entry also proves an exact rank formula for threshold-column matrices, an explicit two-by-two example at 2,3,5, separation in the two-prime comparison, and the four-base dyadic recurrence for the actual 2,3,5 sum. A uniform finite-rank approximation statement concerns the rescaled carry matrix. The stronger unit-determinant modular minors are in E269_08 and are outside this configuration. Infinite kernel rank does not prove irrationality of the running-LCM series. In the selected rank theorem the determinants remain nonzero for every fixed third exponent k using the same injective row and column maps. The distance theorem concerns a rescaled real carry matrix and is not an approximation lower bound for the original summable kernel.

candidates.title: Machine-Checked Christofides 3/2-Approximation and Polyhedral Complexity Barriers for the Traveling Salesperson Problem in Lean 4
candidates.abstract: This formalization develops a machine-checked theory of the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) on finite undirected graphs over Fin n in Lean 4 across two principal modules. First, in Christofides.lean (compared against ChallengeChristofides.lean), we formalize the complete Christofides-Serdyukov 3/2-approximation algorithm for Metric TSP: the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) lower bound (cost(T) <= OPT), Euler's handshaking parity invariant for odd-degree vertices, the minimum-weight perfect matching upper bound on odd-degree vertices (2 * cost(M) <= OPT) via alternating matching decomposition of shortcut cycles, multigraph degree parity of T U M, constructive existence of Eulerian circuits via Hierholzer cycle splicing and complete Christofides certificates, metric walk shortcutting contraction, and the unconditional 3/2-approximation guarantee in both exact integer scaling and real arithmetic. Second, in TSPComplexity.lean (compared against ChallengeTSPComplexity.lean), we formalize polyhedral and complexity-theoretic barriers for Decision TSP: a fuel-bounded branch-and-cut state machine with verified soundness, completeness, and support-pruned cycle-separation rank decision equivalence; the Dantzig-Fulkerson-Johnson (DFJ) subtour cut inequality (every valid tour crosses any proper nonempty cut at least twice); the continuous Held-Karp LP relaxation embedding; a machine-checked proof that the 10-vertex Petersen graph fractional assignment (x_e = 2/3) strictly separates the Held-Karp relaxation from the integral TSP polytope with zero slack on singleton cuts and slack >= 2/3 on all nontrivial cuts; Yannakakis DFJ slack matrix nonnegativity and conditional Fiorini-Rothvoss PSD extension complexity scaling; and polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian Cycle and gadget-parameterized 3-SAT to Decision TSP.

candidates.title: The least physical dimension of an inflation-symmetric model set, with the cubic, quartic and degree-12 inflations of x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1
candidates.abstract:
Kernel-checked proofs, in Lean 4 + Mathlib, about cut-and-project schemes on a fixed integer lattice Z^iota invariant under an integer matrix A: splittings R^iota = E + H into A-invariant subspaces with Z^iota meeting H only in 0 and the projection of Z^iota to H dense in H, a window W in H (bounded, containing a relative ball), the model set Lambda(W) = {pi_E g : g in Z^iota, pi_H g in W}, and admissibility, some window with A Lambda(W) contained in Lambda(W) (inflation symmetry in Meyer's inclusion sense). The least physical dimension d(A) is the least dim E over admissible schemes. Thirteen compared theorems. (1) For every integer A, a scheme is admissible iff A is power-bounded on H; then the orbit window is a compact convex symmetric invariant window; the per-window criterion; and U(A) <= dim E, U(A) the number of eigenvalues of modulus > 1. (2) Kronecker's density criterion in cut-and-project form. (3) For every integer A with det A != 0, any chi_A: (a) d(A) is the sum over the distinct irreducible factors p of chi_A over Q of m_p u_p + c_p (m_p - r_1(p)), plus min(deg p, 2) when every root of p lies on the unit circle and r_1(p) = m_p, where m_p is the multiplicity, u_p and c_p count the roots of p of modulus > 1 and = 1, and r_1(p) = (2 dim ker p(A) - dim ker p(A)^2) / deg p (ranks over Q) is the number of Jordan blocks of size one at each root of p; (b) the value is an invariant of rational similarity; (c) the factors with all roots on the unit circle are the cyclotomic ones; and (d) for chi_A squarefree every invariant splitting is E = ker q_E(A), H = ker q_H(A) with chi_A = q_E q_H, it is admissible iff the roots of q_H lie in the closed unit disk and every irreducible rational factor of chi_A shares a root with q_E, and d(A) = U(A) + circleCount(A), counting 1 for each factor x - 1, x + 1 and 2 for each other cyclotomic factor, each with its multiplicity. (4) For det A != 0 and hyperbolic A, any chi_A and no diagonalizability: a scheme is admissible iff E contains the unstable set iff H lies in the stable set; an invariant splitting carries an admissible scheme iff E contains the unstable set; d(A) = U(A), attained only by the unstable/stable splitting. (5) For det A != 0, any chi_A: d(A) = 1 iff chi_A is irreducible with exactly one root of modulus > 1 (a real root, a Pisot or Salem number up to sign, or an integer on Z^1), or A = +-1 in any rank; in the irreducible case every admissible line is the eigenline. (6) If A^k = 1: every factor is cyclotomic and d = sum of min(deg p, 2) over the distinct factors; the same for chi_A squarefree with all roots on the unit circle; every integer matrix with chi_A = Phi_n, n >= 3 (multiplication by a primitive n-th root of unity), needs exactly a plane. (7) Jordan blocks on the circle: I_2 and the Jordan block J_2 both have chi = (x - 1)^2, for which the squarefree count of (3), with x - 1 counted twice, gives 2, but d = 1 and 2; 1 + J_2(1) and 1 + J_3(1) have d = 2 and 3. (8) Multiplication by rho, rho^-1, Q and theta = -Q^-1 = 1 - Q^3 on Z[rho] and Z[Q] (rho^3 = rho + 1, Q^4 = Q + 1): d = 1, 2, 3, 1. (9) On Z[rho] (x) Z[Q] (degree 12), multiplication by every alpha other than 0, +-1 is nonsingular (det != 0) and hyperbolic with d = U; for rho, theta, rho Q and Q the values are 4, 3, 5, 9. (10) rho and theta act on their unstable spaces as real scalars, and the spectral projection carries the quartic (resp. cubic) sector onto them with the Gram pairing GramRho (x) GramQ equal to that of GramQ (resp. GramRho), of types (3,1) and (2,1). (11) The scheme of Q on Z^4 with an interval window: a segment, an explicit Q-invariant model set in R^3, determinant -1/q' on E, non-real moduli, and the types (2,1) and (1,0) of the trace form on E and H. (12) A Salem witness, the companion of x^4 - x^3 - x^2 - x + 1: not hyperbolic, d = 1. (13) Every model set is a Delone set (Mathlib's Delone.DeloneSet) with uniformly discrete difference set. The mathematics of (1), (2), (4), (5) for irreducible chi_A, and (13), and of (6) for chi_A = Phi_n, is known in other formulations (Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova 2021; Kronecker, Pleasants 2000; Harriss-Koivusalo-Walton 2025, preprint; Meyer 1972, 1995; Lagarias 1999; Solomyak 2020; the classical cyclotomic model sets; Moody 1997); (1) and (4) are stated with no diagonalizability hypothesis. The scheme and model set of (11) are, in substance, instances of Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova Thm 13.1 and of Harriss-Koivusalo-Walton Section 3.4, and are not new. For squarefree chi_A the count of (3) also follows from the arguments of Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova (Lemma 5.1, Prop. 8.1(iii), Cor. 13.4), stated there for generic (aperiodic) schemes; the lattice-first least physical dimension was not found stated in the sources read (search completed 2026-10-20). Beyond the cited cases, the entry proves the least physical dimension for every nonsingular integer matrix (3), including what lies outside the diagonalizable class of Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova: a Jordan block of size >= 2 at an eigenvalue on the unit circle counts in full (the terms c_p (m_p - r_1(p)), which vanish for diagonalizable A), and at a cyclotomic factor with such a block the blocks of size one cost nothing, the internal space being tilted into the socle of the larger blocks; the witnesses are J_2, 1 + J_2(1) and 1 + J_3(1) (7). Every admissible scheme of an A with such a block at a root of unity has Z^iota meeting E in a nonzero vector. It also proves the characterization of every admissible splitting for squarefree chi_A ((3)(d)), non-generic splittings included (its necessity half is the injectivity argument of Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova, Lemma 5.1), and (1) for every integer matrix and (4) for every nonsingular hyperbolic integer matrix, with no diagonalizability hypothesis; for diagonalizable A and generic schemes, the uniqueness of the minimal scheme in (4) and of the minimal physical line in (5) is immediate from Masakova-Mazac-Pelantova, Cor. 13.4. For det A != 0 and squarefree chi_A with a factor Phi_n, n not in {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}, the minimal scheme is not unique, by (3)(d). The companion matrices are multiplication by rho and Q in the power bases by definition, so Crho^i (x) CQ^j is multiplication by rho^i Q^j in the product basis. That the rho^i Q^j are a Z-basis of the ring of integers of Q(rho, Q) is statement (8) of the author's registered entry PALOMAR-2026-10-21-000012 (stalex444/pdt-hermite-signature-compositum@5aa870e98236ba240561b798265c629df8c2d031); that GramRho, GramQ and GramRho (x) GramQ are the Gram matrices of the trace forms in these bases is statements (8), (9) and (19) of the author's registered entry PALOMAR-2026-09-02-000014, in which Q(rho) (x) Q(Q) is the field Q(rho, Q) (its (23)). These are cited, not compared. Application (cited, not a claim of the entry): In the author's Pisot Dimensional Theory, Q(rho) is the arithmetic of three-dimensional space and Q(Q) the arithmetic of four-dimensional spacetime, and their compositum K, whose integers are Z[rho] (x) Z[Q], is the parent of both (the author's registered entry PALOMAR-2026-10-21-000012 (stalex444/pdt-hermite-signature-compositum@5aa870e98236ba240561b798265c629df8c2d031), statements (7), (8)). A model set is the shadow of a lattice cut through a window, a standard mathematical model of a quasicrystal (Moody 2000). Read through the theory, this entry's theorems fix how many dimensions each of the theory's inflations needs to be the symmetry of one, and which ones.
Space inflates the parent through spacetime, and spacetime inflates it through space. On the parent's lattice the plastic inflation rho needs exactly four physical dimensions, and only one scheme attains four (4, 9). Those four are a copy of spacetime's: rho has a single expanding embedding in Q(rho), the real one, and the spectral projection maps the quartic sector onto them, carrying Z[Q] with its trace form unchanged, of Lorentzian type (3,1) (10). rho acts on them as a pure dilation by rho = 1.3247..., the same stretch in every direction (10). Symmetrically, the unit theta = -Q^-1 = 1 - Q^3 needs exactly three, and those three are a copy of space's: Q(rho)'s real space with its form of type (2,1) unchanged, dilated by t = -1/q' = 1.3803... (8, 9, 10). Taken over all three embeddings of Q(rho) instead of the one expanding embedding, the form on the quartic sector is tripled: the factor 3 of statement (13) of PALOMAR-2026-10-21-000012.
The clock needs one dimension; the ruler needs five. On Z[rho] the plastic inflation needs exactly one: the line, over a two-dimensional window at the complex place (8). The plastic substitution's control-point sets are regular model sets in this scheme, with Rauzy-fractal windows in C (Baake and Grimm 2020), and in the theory the line is time and its points are the ticks (PALOMAR-2026-08-19-000006, PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000019). The coupling ruler rho Q, which generates the parent field (Q(rho Q) = K; statement (15) of PALOMAR-2026-10-21-000012, where Z[rho Q] has index 53 in the integers; PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005), needs exactly five, over a seven-dimensional window (9): one real and two complex expanding places, a dimension neither sector has.
The parent holds no circle, so every minimal scheme is forced. Off the parent, eigenvalues on the unit circle can change the count: a Salem inflation's circle eigendirections lie in the internal space and cost nothing, so it still needs only a line (5, 12), but multiplication by a primitive n-th root of unity, n >= 3, needs exactly a plane, and every element of finite order n >= 3 needs at least one (6). The parent has none. No element of K other than +-1 has a conjugate on the unit circle (statement (17) of PALOMAR-2026-10-21-000012), so every inflation of the parent by an element other than 0 and +-1 is hyperbolic, needs exactly as many dimensions as it has expanding embeddings (a complex place counts twice), and has a unique minimal scheme (4, 9).

candidates.title: Hermite's signature theorem and the coprime compositum, with the degree-12 compositum of x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1
candidates.abstract:
Kernel-checked proofs, in Lean 4 + Mathlib, of six general theorems and twelve statements about one number field. General: (1) Hermite's signature theorem for every real polynomial f, degenerate case included and with no monic hypothesis: the power-sum Hankel (Hermite) form H_f has sigPos = #R + #C+, sigNeg = #C+, rank sigPos + sigNeg = #D and radical of dimension deg f - #D, where D, R, C+ are the distinct complex roots, the real ones, and those in the upper half plane; (2) its number-field form (classical, Hermite-Sylvester; in number-field form credited to O. Taussky 1968): the trace form Tr_{K/Q}(x^2) of a number field K has type (r1 + r2, r2), and is positive definite iff K is totally real; (3) the places of a linearly disjoint compositum L = K1 K2: r1(L) = r1(K1) r1(K2) and 2 r2(L) = [K1:Q][K2:Q] - r1(K1) r1(K2); (4) the signed discriminant of such a compositum with coprime discriminants, d_L = d_{K1}^[K2:Q] d_{K2}^[K1:Q], the sign included; (5) the trace projection [E:F]^-1 Tr_{E/F} onto a subfield F, the orthogonal decomposition E = F + F^perp for Tr_{E/Q}(xy) with F^perp = ker Tr_{E/F}, the restriction of the trace form of E to F as [E:F] times the trace form of F, and the type (r1(E) + r2(E) - r1(F) - r2(F), r2(E) - r2(F)) of its restriction to ker Tr_{E/F}; (6) the squarefree-discriminant criterion (a textbook exercise). The field: the compositum L of Q(rho) and Q(Q), rho and Q roots of x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1, built as the tower K3 = Q[X]/(X^3 - X - 1), L = K3[Y]/(Y^4 - Y - 1), of degree 12: (7) the setting (degrees 3, 4, 12; linearly disjoint sectors); (8) O_{Q(rho)} = Z[rho], O_{Q(Q)} = Z[Q], discriminants -23 and -283, O_L = Z[rho, Q] with basis rho^i Q^j; (9) d_L = (-23)^4 (-283)^3 = -6342648595267; (10) places (1,1), (2,1), (2,5) and the trace-form type (7,5) of L, derived from (2) and (3) with no root located; (11) the relative traces on the product basis; (12) Tr(-alpha^-1) = 1 for alpha^n = alpha + 1 in degree n, the unit sections -Q^-1 and -rho^-1 of the relative traces, their surjectivity on rings of integers and the integral splittings of ranks 3 + 9 and 4 + 8; (13) the orthogonal decompositions of L along the two sectors, with restrictions 4 Tr and 3 Tr of types (2,1), (3,1) and complements of types (5,4), (4,4); (14) the covolume 2^-5 23^2 283 sqrt(283) of O_L in Mathlib's normalization, which is 4 times the product covol(O_{Q(rho)})^4 covol(O_{Q(Q)})^3; (15) the discriminant -23^4 53^2 283^3 of the degree-12 polynomial, which is the minimal polynomial of rho Q, and the index [O_L : Z[rho Q]] = 53; (16) the subfield lattice {Q, Q(rho), Q(Q), L}; (17) root-rigidity and circle-freeness of L; (18) Smyth's lower bound for the Mahler measure on O_L, with Smyth's theorem as an explicit hypothesis (cited, not proved). Eighteen compared theorems. The mathematics of (1)-(6) is classical and no novelty is claimed for it; the contribution is the kernel-checked proofs: (1), (2) and (5) from Mathlib's sigPos, sigNeg (D. Loeffler) and, for (2) and (5), Algebra.traceForm, between which Mathlib has no theorem at the pinned revision; (3) and (4) from Mathlib's infinite places and linear disjointness. The proof modules also prove, not compared, that sigPos and sigNeg are additive over orthogonal direct sums and invariant under positive scaling over any linearly ordered field, and that the signature of a rational matrix form is unchanged by base change to R; Mathlib at the pin has none of these. Mathlib prior art is used and not re-proved: X. Roblot's theorem on the absolute value of the discriminant of a coprime compositum (statement (4) adds the sign) and his theorem on its ring of integers (used in (8)). The definiteness corollary of (1) (real-rooted iff H_f positive semidefinite) was formalized in Lean 4 by P. Alexandersson (RealRooted, 2026-09-27) before this entry; (1) proves the full rank/signature/radical count, from which that corollary follows. No prior formalization of the rank and signature count of the Hermite form, or of the trace-form signature (r1 + r2, r2) of a number field, was found by a search on 2026-10-19 (Mathlib, the Isabelle AFP, Coq/MathComp, HOL Light, Lean 4 community repositories, Zenodo, arXiv); the existing root-counting formalizations use sign variations of remainder sequences. The sector inputs of the field at the level of Q are ported from the author's registered entry PALOMAR-2026-09-02-000014 and are not compared; (7) and the minimal-polynomial clause of (15) re-prove facts certified in the author's registered entry PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005 and are not new. Application (cited, not a claim of the entry): In the author's Pisot Dimensional Theory, Q(rho) is the arithmetic of three-dimensional space and Q(Q) the arithmetic of four-dimensional spacetime, and their compositum K is the parent of both. Read through the theory, this entry's theorems make six conclusions exact.
Space and spacetime are the only worlds the parent contains. The fields between Q and K have degrees 3 and 4 and no others: Q(rho) and Q(Q) are K's only proper subfields other than Q (16). An intermediate sub-arithmetic of the parent has dimension 3 or 4, and nothing else; there is no 2-, 6- or other intermediate world.
The world is a product, not a sum. K is the tensor product of the two sectors, 12 = 3*4 (7), and its integers are exactly Z[rho] (x) Z[Q] (8). The parent's discrete structure is built from the two sectors' lattices and nothing else.
The parent's geometry is the product of space's and spacetime's. The trace form of K has type (7,5) (10), and it is the tensor product of the sectors' own forms (PALOMAR-2026-09-02-000014): (2,1) (x) (3,1), with 2*3 + 1*1 = 7 and 2*1 + 1*3 = 5. On the quartic sector the form is 3 times spacetime's own, of Lorentzian type (3,1); on the cubic sector, 4 times space's, of type (2,1) (13). The one time direction is not put in by hand: it is what the parent's form is on spacetime.
All of the parent's asymmetry between space and time is spacetime's. The parent's excess of positive over negative directions, 7 - 5 = 2, is exactly spacetime's 3 - 1 = 2. The eight dimensions orthogonal to spacetime are perfectly balanced, four positive and four negative (5, 13).
Both sectors are recovered from the parent. The relative traces, divided by the relative degrees [K:Q(rho)] = 4 and [K:Q(Q)] = 3, are the orthogonal projections onto the sectors (5), and the traces themselves carry the parent's lattice onto Z[rho] and Z[Q] (12). Every element of space and of spacetime is the shadow of an element of the parent.
The parent is built from minimizers, and joining them creates nothing smaller. Each sector's generator is a minimizer, certified in the author's registered entries: x^3 - x - 1 and x^4 - x - 1 attain the least Mahler measure above 1 among irreducible integer polynomials of degrees 3 and 4 (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004); rho is the least Pisot eigenvalue of any substitution on at most three letters, the slowest settling clock (PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000019), and the growth rate of the triangle group (2,3,infinity) = PGL(2,Z), the slowest of the hyperbolic triangle groups (p,q,infinity) (PALOMAR-2026-10-17-000013). K is the compositum of the two minimizers, and a single number generates all of it: rho*Q, the theory's coupling ruler (15; PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005). Minimality survives the join. No element of K other than +/-1 has a conjugate on the unit circle (17), so the parent contains no Salem number, and with Smyth's theorem every nonzero integer of K other than +/-1 has Mahler measure at least rho (18), with equality at rho itself (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004). The 3D generator is the smallest nontrivial size in the whole twelve-dimensional arithmetic, exactly as in degree 3. In the theory, rho is the ground of minimality and therefore the ground of three-dimensional structure; joining space to spacetime keeps that ground.
The two sectors are the two sides of the Pisot boundary. rho is a Pisot number, and the Padovan substitution tiling, whose characteristic polynomial is x^3 - x - 1, is a regular model set with pure-point diffraction (Baake and Grimm 2020): the ordered, classical sector. It is handed, the arrow of time: its tiling flow is neither mutually locally derivable from nor topologically conjugate to its mirror image (Gaehler 2026, Example 10 and Remark 7, where the Padovan rule is varrho_R after renaming a <-> c), and in the factor language the author's registered entries PALOMAR-2026-08-19-000006, PALOMAR-2026-09-04-000004 and PALOMAR-2026-10-18-000019 certify it: ca occurs and ac never does. Q is not Pisot (PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000012), and every primitive self-similar tiling of the line with expansion Q has no non-trivial pure-point spectrum (Solomyak 1997): the quantum sector, which cannot settle on a line. This is the arithmetic of a quasicrystal (superspace crystallography: de Wolff 1974; Janner and Janssen 1977; cut-and-project: de Bruijn 1981; Kramer and Neri 1984; Duneau and Katz 1985; Elser 1986): a higher-dimensional lattice, O_K in R^2 x C^5, from which the sector lattices are recovered by the traces (12).

candidates.title: Finite correlated equilibria and regret certificates
candidates.abstract: For finite games with player-specific action types, a valid independent product distribution is a correlated equilibrium exactly when its mixed profile is Nash. The correlated-equilibrium set is nonempty, compact, and convex when every player's action type is nonempty. For every positive finite horizon, cumulative external-regret and swap-regret bounds give corresponding approximate coarse-correlated and correlated equilibria of the empirical distribution. The development also proves equivalence with conditional obedience inequalities, arbitrary mixed-deviation sufficiency, and extension-by-zero correspondence for restricted legal actions. An exact per-recommendation certificate characterizes approximate correlated equilibrium without loss in its error budget and directly certifies empirical play from cumulative recommendation gains.

candidates.title: Clique partitions of chordal graphs: quantitative stability and sharp eventual bounds
candidates.abstract: A Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the chordal results of the author's preprint "Clique partitions with rooted simplicial defect: quantitative stability and sharp eventual bounds" (Erdős #81 series, Paper IV). With M(n) = ⌊n(n+1)/6⌋: there is b such that every chordal graph on n vertices has a clique partition into pieces of order at most four with at most M(n) + b pieces (Theorem A); for n large every chordal graph on n vertices has one with at most M(n) pieces, and some chordal graph on n vertices has one with exactly M(n) pieces that is optimal among all clique partitions (Theorem B, the bound asked in Erdős Problem #81 and its sharpness); 1/6 is the least quadratic coefficient (§6.3); the uniform mixed rounding of fractional triangle/K₄ packings (Theorem 3.1); integral stability with explicit constants and edit distance at most 16δ to a complete-split graph, for 0 ≤ δ ≤ γn² with γ = 10⁻¹⁶/4 (Theorem 6.1); same-root control of near-optimal partitions: one clique root satisfies all the conclusions of Theorem 6.1 and, for it, every partition with at most M(n) + τ pieces has at most τ + 48δ noncanonical pieces (Corollary 6.1a); the root-defect identity (6.7b); and the eventual classification of the extremal chordal graphs as complete-split graphs with a core of optimal size (Corollary 6.2). Eight statements. The thresholds N are existential; b and N are not claimed optimal.

candidates.title: The Dancing Sand Theorem: the 2-part of the sandpile group of the hypercube, for every n
candidates.abstract: Let $K (Q_{n})$ be the sandpile group (critical group, Jacobian) of the $n$-dimensional hypercube graph $Q_{n}$. Its odd part was determined by Bai in 2003; its $2$-part has been open since then. Gao, Marx-Kuo, McDonald and Yuen determined its $n - 1$ largest cyclic factors, and Betzer the $n$-th, through a remark of theirs stated without proof. We determine the whole 2-part of $K (Q_{n})$ for every $n$, by an explicit rule. The group splits over the indecomposable tilting modules $T (\lambda)$ of $\mathrm{SL}_{2}$ in characteristic $2$ that occur in $V^{\otimes n}$, with their multiplicities. The contribution of $T (\lambda)$ at the shift $i = (n - \lambda) / 2$ consists of explicit small cyclic factors and of $2^{| I |}$ large ones, where $I$ is the set of binary digits of $\lambda + 1$ below the leading one. The large ones are obtained by pooling a sequence of explicit integers — binomial valuations and carries — into a non-increasing sequence, in the manner of isotonic regression. The proof reduces each contribution, by elimination inside explicit $2$-adic lattices, to the Smith form of an explicit $2^{| I |} \times 2^{| I |}$ integer matrix, and computes that Smith form from the valuations of its entries. It needs a unique cheapest matching for an upper bound and an inductive potential for a lower bound. As consequences we recover Bai's counts and the theorems of Gao, Marx-Kuo, McDonald and Yuen on the largest factors, we prove their Conjecture 4.14 without that remark, and we prove their Conjecture 5.4 and the formula for the $(n + 1)$-th factor stated in the 2019 poster of three of them. We also prove the fold law: the 2-part of the sandpile group of the folded cube $Q_{n} / \langle (1, \dots, 1) \rangle$ is $2 \cdot \operatorname{Syl}_{2} K (Q_{n})$, the group obtained by lowering every exponent by one. With the results above this gives the whole $2$-part of the sandpile group of the folded cube, and, with the known odd part, its whole sandpile group. The whole proof has been checked in the proof assistant Lean 4 with the Mathlib library, with nothing cited. This work has not been refereed by a human expert.

candidates.title: Optimal packings of one to seven unit squares in a disk
candidates.abstract: For n = 1, …, 7: the least radius of a closed disk holding n unit squares with disjoint interiors, each placed and rotated freely, and every packing that attains it. The radii are √2/2, √5/2, 5√17/16, √2, √(5/2), √q* ≈ 1.68854 and √13/2, where q* is a quartic irrational. Up to rotation about the disk centre and relabelling, the optimal packing is unique for n ≤ 6: the square, the 2 × 1 rectangle, the T, the 2 × 2 block, the plus, and for six squares a central square with four neighbours, two of them pushed along its sides, and a sixth square turned by π/4 between those two. For n = 7 the optimal packings form a three-parameter family: two columns of two squares and, between them, a column of three whose heights vary independently, at least 1 apart and within √3 − 1/2 of the disk centre. The proofs for three to six squares bound the arcs the squares occupy on a small circle about the disk centre. For six squares this finds the square that contains the disk centre; five fixed points label the others, and a weighted sum of separating inequalities, with estimates uniform in the angles of the squares, forces the optimal radius. For seven squares, each square avoiding the disk centre gets a direction from it, and in the optimal disk two disjoint such squares get directions at least π/3 apart. We found no earlier proof for five, six or seven squares, and no exact one for three, where a computer-assisted enclosure of the radius and the optimal arrangements was known. Four squares, uniqueness included, were settled by hand in 2026, by the same idea as here.

candidates.title: The Critical 2D KPZ Process
candidates.abstract: A Lean 4 formalization of "The Critical 2D KPZ Process" by Berger, Caravenna, Clark, Dunlap, Gu, Liu, Nakajima, Sun, Tsai, Xie and Zygouras (arXiv:2610.31614, version 1), together with selected inputs and adaptations in the form these proofs need. For directed polymers on Z^2 in a Gaussian environment at critical disorder, it proves the existence of a critical 2D stochastic heat flow, defined as the joint limit in law of the rescaled partition functions (Theorem A). The centred log-partition function converges in law, in the local negative Sobolev spaces H^{-a}_loc and jointly in finitely many times and initial data, to the critical 2D KPZ process (Theorem 1.2). The process satisfies the comparison principle in the initial data. For flat initial data, its averages at scale epsilon, divided by sqrt(log log(1/epsilon)), converge in law to a centred Gaussian (Theorem 1.4(i)); it has a radial covariance kernel equivalent to log log(1/|z|) at the diagonal (Theorem 1.4(ii)), is not a signed measure (Proposition 1.5), is not Gaussian (Theorem 1.6), is invariant under translations and rotations and covariant under scaling (Proposition 1.8), and its pairing with each nonnegative test function has a law of Ehrhard type (Proposition 3.8). It also proves strict skewness, twice differentiable response to initial data, Brownian motion across scales and the finite-dimensional GFF tangent (Theorems A–D of Scott Armstrong’s note). The parameter theta is fixed. Built on Mathlib. All proofs use only Lean's standard axioms.

candidates.title: De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory under coarse ellipticity
candidates.abstract: A Lean 4 formalization of the paper "Coarse ellipticity and De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory in the optimal range" by S. Armstrong, B. Avelin, T. Kuusi and A. Turpeinen (arXiv:2610.11879). The paper extends the theory of De Giorgi–Nash–Moser to elliptic equations with symmetric coefficients a(x) which are possibly degenerate and unbounded but satisfy a coarse ellipticity condition: spatial moments of coarse-grained matrices, suitably discounted and summed across scales, are finite. Under this condition it proves local upper bounds for weak subsolutions, a weak Harnack inequality for nonnegative supersolutions, and a Harnack inequality for nonnegative solutions. The condition holds if a ∈ W^{-α,p} ∩ L^1, a^{-1} ∈ W^{-β,q} ∩ L^1 and (α+β)/2 + ((d-1)/2)(1/p + 1/q) < 1, for some α, β ≥ 0 and 1 < p, q < ∞. This range is sharp, including its boundary, in every dimension d ≥ 3: for α = β = 0, where it corresponds to the results of Bella and Schäffner, and for the corresponding Besov-type quasi-norms of negative order when α, β > 0. The formalization covers these results, together with the optimality of the powers of the coarse ellipticity ratio in the local bounds and of the range of exponents in the weak Harnack inequality. The statements are for dimension d ≥ 3 and are formulated on the unit cube; the limiting cases p = ∞ or q = ∞ are not formalized. CORRESPONDENCE.md gives the status of every numbered statement of the paper. Built on Mathlib and the CoarseGraining library, using only Lean's standard axioms.

candidates.title: The golden family's boundary at n = 3: general-n theorems for x^n = x + 1
candidates.abstract: Kernel-checked general-n theorems for the golden family — the ladder of trinomials x^n - x - 1, whose unique real root r_n > 1 descends from the golden ratio (n = 2) through the plastic number (n = 3) toward 1. The family's structural boundary falls at n = 3; this entry proves the morphic half unconditionally at general n and holds the Pisot half as the measure⟺Pisot equivalence, the unconditional n = 4 non-Pisot statement, and the Siegel-conditional strict excess for n >= 4, from the family's own arithmetic, with no per-degree case check above the boundary. Eleven compared statements carry the surface. (1) The root ladder: for every n >= 2 the root exists, is unique above 1, and strictly decreases in n. (2) The morphic boundary, UNCONDITIONAL: r_n satisfies the golden ratio's two scale closures p + 1 = p^k and p - 1 = p^(-l) (Aarts-Fokkink-Kruijtzer 2001, spelled inline) if and only if n <= 3 — the classification pins morphic numbers to the golden ratio and the plastic number, and descent puts r_n below 1.23, hence below both, for n >= 4. (3) Circle exclusion: x^n - x - 1 has no complex root of modulus 1, for any n (|z| = |z + 1| = 1 forces z^2 + z + 1 = 0, so z^3 = 1, and every residue of n mod 3 is impossible). (4) The Jensen lower bound r_n <= M(x^n - x - 1), by the monic root-product form of the Mahler measure. (5) The equivalence M(x^n - x - 1) = r_n iff every other complex root lies strictly inside the unit circle — the honest form of "the family's Mahler-measure boundary IS its Pisot boundary": the equivalence is itself the kernel theorem (exact because the family never has unimodular roots, and its trinomials are separable by Selmer irreducibility), stated once and never counted as a pair of separate boundaries. (6) The Siegel-conditional closure: IF the plastic number is the smallest Pisot number — Siegel 1944, entering ONLY as an explicit named hypothesis, with "Pisot" unfolded in the statement — THEN r_n < M(x^n - x - 1) for every n >= 4. Siegel's minimality is the single classical input anywhere in the entry; every other statement is kernel-checked unconditionally, and Siegel's theorem itself is not proved here. (7) Q < psi: the quartic root (q^4 = q + 1) lies strictly below psi (psi^4 = psi^3 + 1), the Mahler measure of the n = 4 member. (8) THE SHARED LEMMA, at general n: no root of x^n - x - 1 satisfies z^2 + z + 1 = 0 (z^3 = 1 and every residue of n mod 3 is impossible). It supplies the obstruction in the circle exclusion (3), which is re-derived from it as an explicit corollary (the circle geometry supplies the reduction), and up to the substitution z^n = z + 1 (under which z^n + z^2 = 0 iff z^2 + z + 1 = 0) it is Mathlib's public Polynomial.X_pow_sub_X_sub_one_irreducible_aux — the first step of Mathlib's Selmer proof, hence of the morphic classification behind (2) — restated in the family's own vocabulary; compared as the named shared core, not as new mathematics. (9) Witness b_3 (b^3 = b^2 + 1): every other complex root of x^3 = x^2 + 1 has modulus < 1, and b_3 is not morphic. (10) Witness psi (psi^4 = psi^3 + 1): every other complex root of x^4 = x^3 + 1 has modulus < 1, and psi is not morphic. (11) The golden quartic root is NOT Pisot: for q^4 = q + 1, some complex root of x^4 = x + 1 other than q has modulus > 1 (every nonreal root does — quartic_conj_norm_gt_one in the proof module, not compared) — with (10) and (7) the degree-4 separation: Q and psi are both algebraic units with constant term of modulus one (unit-ness is elementary and not compared: Q^-1 = Q^3 - 1, psi^-1 = psi^3 - psi^2), yet Q is not Pisot and psi is, so the unit condition alone does not locate the Pisot boundary. (10) and (11) are not independent evidence: x^4 - x^3 - 1 is the image of x^4 - x - 1 under x -> -1/x, so the Pisot half of (10) says x^4 - x - 1 has one root inside the unit circle and three outside, and (11) follows; they are compared separately for the two families' sakes. THE STORY: one shared lemma beneath both boundaries (naming the family-specific arithmetic core, not the whole proof graph: (2) and (6) also share the elementary descent r_n < 1.23 < rho, and the kernel-held Pisot side is localized by Siegel plus descent, the angle route being context); the boundaries localize by different routes — an angle for Pisot (the escape arc between the primitive cube roots of unity, giving the outside-root count 1 + 2*floor((2n - 1)/6), Howell-Kyle 2018 Theorem 3 via the reciprocal trinomial; context, NOT formalized), a degree for morphic (the cofactor x^2 - x + 1 forcing k = 3; formalized) — and the classes are in fact separable: (9)-(11) hold the witnesses and the degree-4 separation in the kernel, with no Siegel input, showing the classes coming apart inside the sister trinomial family itself (Pisot units below phi that are not morphic). The entry never claims the two boundaries are independent (they share the lemma) and never claims a common cause for their location. Two spellings of "Pisot" appear: the trinomial-roots form of (5), (9), (10), (11) and the minimal-polynomial form of the siegel hypothesis; they coincide exactly when the defining trinomial is irreducible (Selmer for (5), (11); x^3 - x^2 - 1 and x^4 - x^3 - 1 have no rational root and no integer quadratic factorization, for (9), (10)). On the sister family x^m - x^(m-1) - 1 the classes come apart: b_2 = phi and b_5 = rho exactly, so morphic only for m = 2, 5 (AFK, kernel-held, plus strict decrease); Pisot at m = 2, 5 is elementary, though at m = 5 the quintic is reducible with two roots ON the unit circle, so b_5 is Pisot in the minimal-polynomial sense only; the m = 3, 4 members are the kernel-held witnesses; not Pisot for 6 <= m <= 30 numerically and for all m >= 6 Siegel-conditionally (b_6 < rho). The n <= 4 instances of this boundary are registered content of the author's sibling entries (PALOMAR-2026-08-31-000004, PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000005, and PALOMAR-2026-09-01-000008) and are cited as context imports, never re-compared. The classical route to the n >= 4 strict excess (Smyth 1971), the limit behavior of the family measures (Lawton 1983, Smyth 1981, Verger-Gaugry 2016, Stankov 2014), and the outside-root count (Howell-Kyle 2018, with Brilleslyper-Schaubroeck 2014 for the unimodular criterion and Stankov 2014 for the asymptotic density) are cited context, not formalized — see the labeled context block in the sources. As of the 2026-09-01 sweep the entry is not aware of a prior formalization of the general-n family boundary, of Siegel minimality, of Smyth's nonreciprocal bound, or of Pisot-number theory in any surveyed prover ecosystem; Mathlib supplies Selmer irreducibility and the Mahler-measure development as infrastructure. Axioms on every compared theorem: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound, audited in-build.

candidates.title: Almost all Markoff numbers are unique.
candidates.abstract:
A Markoff number is the largest coordinate of a positive integer solution of
$a^2+b^2+c^2=3abc$. Frobenius conjectured in 1913 that every Markoff number
is the largest coordinate of exactly one such solution with $a\le b\le c$.
We prove that the conjecture holds for almost all Markoff numbers: the
proportion of exceptions among the Markoff numbers up to $X$ tends to $0$
as $X\to\infty$.

Two such solutions with the same largest coordinate give simple closed
geodesics of equal length on the modular torus, that is, primitive homology
classes $v,w$ with equal values $N(v)=N(w)$ of the McShane--Rivin stable
norm $N$. Estimates for the boundary of the unit ball of $N$ reduce the
problem to the equations $N(Gv)=N(v)$ with $G$ a rational linear map. For
each $G$ that is not a symmetry of the torus, a zero-one law for the
$3$-adic analytic dynamics of the mapping class group on the Markoff
surface shows that the solutions $v$ have density zero.

candidates.title: sloisel/MPE-Formal
candidates.abstract: Machine-checked proofs of three probabilistic convergence theorems for restarted Minimal Polynomial Extrapolation (MPE) applied to nonlinear fixed-point iterations.  Dithered restarts keep the error below the doubly exponential schedule delta^(theta^m), for any theta in (1,2), from every starting point -- the breakdown set included -- with an explicit failure-probability exponent over the dither; in the root sense the convergence order is at least theta.  Under simple spectrum, the error follows a quadratically shrinking dither schedule (root order at least 2) with failure probability linear in the initial radius up to a logarithmic factor, and MPE coincides with Reduced Rank Extrapolation at every cycle. With no dither at all, the restarted iteration from a single uniformly random starting point at worst squares the error at every cycle with high probability, under two checkable hypotheses on the Jacobian and the quadratic Taylor coefficients.  The registered statements are self-contained over mathlib: every object of the construction is introduced by an explicit defining equation among the hypotheses.
